title: Continuous variable distributed quantum sensing in integrated photonics
authors: Bethany Puzio, Oliver M. Green, Joel F. Tasker, Jonathan Frazer, Tamzin Ellis, Benjamin D. J. Sayers, Rachel N. Clark, Alex S. Clark, Giacomo Ferranti, Jonathan C. F. Matthews
abstract: Distributed quantum sensing is an emerging application of quantum networking, where entangled probe states are employed to sense combinations of delocalized parameters with enhanced precision relative to using separable states. Squeezed states of light are a prime resource for experimental demonstrations of entanglement-enhanced sensing, because they can be generated and entangled deterministically. Existing distributed quantum sensing experiments have been fundamentally limited in scalability due to their bulk-optic architectures. Meanwhile, integrated photonics provides a scalable and compact platform for quantum sensors. Here we demonstrate entanglement-enhanced sensing of linear functions of four phase shifts in an integrated photonic circuit. We find an entanglement-enhanced precision of 0.199(16) dB below the shot noise limit compared to 0.041(18) dB for separable states. A four-mode entangled state is generated on-chip with entanglement verification and phase sensing also performed on-chip with an array of four integrated homodyne detectors.
summary: This paper demonstrates entanglement-enhanced distributed quantum sensing using continuous variable light implemented on a scalable Silicon-on-Insulator photonic chip. By generating and measuring four-mode entanglement, the authors achieved a significantly higher precision in phase estimation compared to classical methods. This work advances the field by proving the feasibility of quantum sensing in compact, integrated optical hardware.
main_problem: The paper aims to demonstrate and quantify the advantage of using continuous variable (CV) distributed quantum sensing with entangled states over classical (separable) states for measuring phase shifts.
main_result: The entangled sensing protocol achieved a precision of 0.199(16) dB below the shot noise limit, significantly outperforming the separable state limit of 0.041(18) dB.
method: The sensing relies on measuring the DC offset in integrated homodyne detectors after generating a four-mode entangled state on a photonic chip, allowing for the estimation of the average phase shift.
model_or_system: The experiment uses a Silicon-on-Insulator (SOI) Photonic Integrated Circuit (PIC) containing a Beam Splitter Network (BSN) and four integrated homodyne detectors. Entanglement is generated from an off-chip squeezed vacuum source.
key_observables: Mean subtracted photocurrent ($\langle\delta\hat{i}_jangle$), average phase shift ($\phi_{avg}$), and the measured phase variance ($\Delta^2\varphi_{avg}$).
important_parameters: Number of modes ($M=4$), total system efficiency ($\eta = 0.203(5)$), and the comparison between entangled and separable state precision limits.
main_assumptions: The primary limitation noted is the loss introduced by coupling the squeezed light on or off the chip, which limits the achievable performance.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the PIC schematic, the process of converting raw time-domain data into well-defined quadratures, and comparative plots showing the measured phase precision advantage for both entangled and separable states.
paper_structure: The paper details the physical setup (SOI PIC, BSN, detectors), the theoretical framework for precision calculation ($\sigma_e$ vs $\sigma_s$), the measurement techniques (noise locking, quadrature extraction), and finally presents the quantitative comparison of sensing performance.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, scalable, and integrated platform demonstration of quantum metrology principles, directly advancing the hardware realization of quantum sensing protocols.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: The photonic chip (A) Layout of the silicon-on-insulator (SOI) photonic integrated circuit (PIC). The single mode squeezed vacuum and local oscillator (LO) are coupled onto the PIC via grating couplers. Entanglement is generated across four spatial modes by mixing the squeezed light with vacuum across three cascaded Mach-Zehnder interferometers (MZIs). The LO is also split across four spatial modes via MZIs, and then routed to homodyne detectors HD1-4, to detect each mode of the entangled state. Thermo-optic phase modulators (TOPMs) θ1−4 are used to balance HD1-4 respectively, while also acting as the phase parameters to be sensed. (B) Optical microscope image of the PIC and...

Each homodyne detector output is wirebonded to a TIA mounted on a PCB. All TIA outputs are measured on the oscilloscope (scope). HD2 output is split into three paths using power splitters (PS) and an RF amplifier (RF amp) to derive the locking signal whilst measuring output simultaneously on the ESA and the oscilloscope.
